prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

WASHINGTON (CNN)  -- The House of Representatives on Tuesday passed a bill that would make suing for pay discrimination easier by altering a time limit on such suits. The act is named for Lilly Ledbetter, seen here in 2008. Her discrimination lawsuit victory was overturned in 2007. The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, which passed 250-177, would give workers alleging unequal pay the right to sue within 180 days of their most recent paycheck. Current law says such employees must sue within 180 days of receiving their first unfair paycheck. Supporters of the new legislation say that, under the current law, an employer merely needs to hide unfair pay practices for three months before being able to continue them without penalty. The act, named for a former Goodyear Tire employee who sued the company for gender discrimination in 1998, would effectively overturn a 2007 Supreme Court decision on the limit. Ledbetter was awarded $360,000 in back pay by a federal judge in Alabama, but the verdict was overturned in a 5-4 Supreme Court ruling in May 2007. The court said that even though she filed her complaint within 180 days of when she first learned that she was getting paid less than comparable male employees, she had failed to file within 180 days of the first unequal paycheck. After Tuesday's House vote, Speaker Nancy Pelosi said the chamber had "taken a bold step" in passing the legislation. "In doing so, it has injected fairness, reason and common sense back into policy," Pelosi said. The legislation, which passed the Senate on Thursday, now goes to President Barack Obama, who has promised to sign it into law. It is the first major piece of legislation Congress has sent to Obama for his approval. On the campaign trail, Obama and Republican nominee Sen. John McCain debated the bill. Obama heavily emphasized what he called the plan's benefits to working women, while McCain criticized it as a boon for trial lawyers. Pelosi said Obama called to congratulate her on the bill's passage. Obama danced with Ledbetter at one of his inaugural balls, and she spoke at the Democrat National Convention at which he accepted his party's nomination. "My case is over -- I will never receive the pay I deserve," Ledbetter said in that speech. "But there will be a far richer reward if we secure fair pay for our children and grandchildren, so that no one will ever again experience the discrimination that I did."

WASHINGTON (CNN) — On Tuesday, the House of Representatives approved legislation intended to make it easier for employees to bring pay-discrimination lawsuits by changing the deadline for filing such claims.

The measure, called the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, is named after Lilly Ledbetter, a former Goodyear Tire worker whose successful discrimination lawsuit was later reversed in 2007. The bill passed the House by a vote of 250-177.

Under the legislation, workers who claim they are being paid unfairly would be allowed to file a lawsuit within 180 days of their latest paycheck. Existing law requires employees to sue within 180 days of the first paycheck affected by discrimination.

Backers of the bill argue that the current rule allows employers to avoid consequences simply by concealing discriminatory pay practices for three months, after which they can continue the practice without being penalized.

Ledbetter sued Goodyear in 1998, alleging sex-based pay discrimination. A federal judge in Alabama awarded her $360,000 in back pay, but the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that ruling in May 2007 in a 5-4 decision. The justices said that although Ledbetter filed her complaint within 180 days of discovering she had been paid less than similar male employees, she had not filed within 180 days of receiving the first unequal paycheck.

Following the House vote, Speaker Nancy Pelosi said lawmakers had “taken a bold step” by passing the bill. “In doing so, it has injected fairness, reason and common sense back into policy,” Pelosi said.

The Senate passed the legislation on Thursday, and it now heads to President Barack Obama, who has said he will sign it. It is the first major bill Congress has sent to Obama for approval.

During the presidential campaign, Obama and Republican nominee Sen. John McCain argued over the proposal. Obama strongly highlighted what he described as its advantages for working women, while McCain denounced it as a benefit for trial attorneys.

Pelosi said Obama called her to offer congratulations after the bill passed. Obama had danced with Ledbetter at one of his inaugural balls, and she also addressed the Democratic National Convention where he accepted the party’s nomination.

“My case is over -- I will never receive the pay I deserve,” Ledbetter said in that convention speech. “But there will be a far richer reward if we secure fair pay for our children and grandchildren, so that no one will ever again experience the discrimination that I did.”

The House of Representatives passed the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, a measure designed to make it easier for workers to challenge pay discrimination in court. The bill changes the deadline for filing pay-discrimination lawsuits by allowing employees to sue within 180 days of receiving their most recent discriminatory paycheck, rather than requiring them to file within 180 days of the employer’s original decision to pay them unfairly.

The legislation was named for Lilly Ledbetter, a former employee of Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. who sued after learning that she had been paid less than male colleagues for years. In 2007, the Supreme Court ruled against her, saying she had waited too long to file her claim because the deadline began when the discriminatory pay decision was first made. Supporters of the new bill argued that workers often do not discover pay disparities until years later and should not be barred from seeking relief simply because the discrimination was hidden.

The Senate had already approved the measure, and President Barack Obama was expected to sign it into law. Its passage effectively overturns the Supreme Court’s 2007 decision and represents the first major piece of legislation sent to Obama’s desk since he took office.

Backers of the bill, including many Democrats and civil rights advocates, said it was an important step toward ensuring equal pay for equal work. They argued that each unfair paycheck should count as a new act of discrimination because it continues the harm to the worker. Opponents, however, warned that the change could expose employers to lawsuits over decisions made many years earlier and could increase litigation.

Despite those concerns, the bill moved forward with strong support from advocates for women’s rights and workplace fairness. Once signed, the law would give employees more time to challenge discriminatory compensation practices and would restore a broader path for workers seeking back pay and damages in unequal-pay cases.

**House passes Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act**

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style report)** — The House of Representatives on Friday passed legislation aimed at making it easier for workers to challenge pay discrimination, moving quickly on a major Democratic priority at the start of the 111th Congress.

The **Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act** passed the House by a vote of **247 to 171**. The bill was named for **Lilly Ledbetter**, a former Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. employee from Alabama who said she was paid less than male colleagues for years because of her sex.

Ledbetter’s case reached the Supreme Court in 2007, but the justices ruled against her in a **5-4 decision**. The Court said she had filed her claim too late under federal law, because the 180-day deadline to bring a discrimination complaint began when the original pay decision was made — even though she continued receiving paychecks affected by that decision years later.

The ruling drew sharp criticism from Democrats and civil rights advocates, who argued that pay discrimination is often hidden from employees and may not be discovered until long after the first discriminatory paycheck. The new bill would effectively reset the filing deadline with each paycheck affected by discriminatory pay.

House Speaker **Nancy Pelosi** praised the vote, saying the measure would restore fairness for workers and help ensure that employees have a real chance to challenge unequal pay. Pelosi and other supporters framed the bill as a response to the Supreme Court decision and a step toward strengthening workplace protections.

President-elect **Barack Obama** also welcomed the House action. Obama, who had supported the legislation during his presidential campaign, said the bill was an important part of ensuring equal pay for equal work and urged Congress to send it to his desk. The measure would later become the first bill Obama signed into law as president.

Republican opponents argued that the legislation could lead to more lawsuits and make it harder for employers to defend old personnel decisions. Supporters countered that workers should not lose the right to sue before they even know discrimination has occurred.

The House vote marked a significant early victory for Democrats, who had made pay equity a central issue following the Supreme Court’s ruling in Ledbetter’s case.

**Congress Sends Obama First Major Bill: Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act**

*Washington* — Congress has sent President Barack Obama the first major piece of legislation of his new administration, approving the **Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act**, a measure designed to make it easier for workers to challenge pay discrimination.

The bill responds to a 2007 Supreme Court decision involving **Lilly Ledbetter**, a former supervisor at a Goodyear tire plant in Alabama who said she was paid less than male colleagues for years. The Court ruled that her lawsuit was filed too late because she did not bring her claim within 180 days of the company’s original discriminatory pay decision.

The new legislation changes that deadline. Under the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act, the clock for filing a pay discrimination claim restarts each time a worker receives a paycheck affected by discrimination. That means employees may file a lawsuit within the legal deadline after receiving any discriminatory paycheck, rather than being limited to the date when the initial pay decision was made.

Supporters say the change is necessary because pay discrimination is often hidden from employees for years. They argue that workers should not lose the right to sue before they even discover they are being paid unfairly.

Opponents contend the measure could expose employers to lawsuits over decisions made long ago, making it harder to defend against claims involving old records or former managers.

The legislation covers discrimination based on sex, race, national origin, age, religion, and disability. President Obama has said he supports the measure and is expected to sign it, making it the first significant law enacted under his presidency.

**Congress Moves to Reverse Supreme Court Ruling With Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act**

*Washington* — Congress has advanced one of the most closely watched civil rights measures of the new political era, the **Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act**, legislation designed to make it easier for workers to challenge wage discrimination and to overturn a controversial 2007 Supreme Court decision that sharply limited the time employees have to file pay-bias claims.

The bill centers on what became known as the **180-day paycheck rule**. Under federal anti-discrimination law, workers generally must file a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission within 180 days of an unlawful employment practice. In pay discrimination cases, the question was whether that clock starts only when an employer first sets a discriminatory salary — often long before an employee discovers the disparity — or whether each discriminatory paycheck renews the filing period.

The Fair Pay Act adopts the latter approach, stating that every paycheck affected by discrimination can constitute a new violation. Supporters say the change is essential because salary information is often confidential, and employees may not learn for years that they have been paid less because of sex, race, age, religion, national origin or disability.

The legislation was named for **Lilly Ledbetter**, a former supervisor at a Goodyear tire plant in Gadsden, Alabama, who became a national symbol of the fight for equal pay. Ledbetter worked for Goodyear for nearly two decades before discovering, through an anonymous note, that she had been paid significantly less than male colleagues doing similar work. She sued, and a jury initially awarded her damages.

But in **2007**, the Supreme Court ruled against her in **Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.**, holding in a 5-4 decision that she had filed her claim too late because the original pay-setting decisions occurred outside the 180-day filing period. The majority said the law required workers to act within 180 days of the employer’s discriminatory decision, not within 180 days of receiving a paycheck affected by that decision.

Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg read a pointed dissent from the bench, arguing that pay discrimination is often hidden and accumulates over time. She urged Congress to correct the court’s interpretation. The Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act was the legislative response.

House Speaker **Nancy Pelosi** praised the bill as a major civil rights measure and a step toward restoring basic workplace fairness. Pelosi said the legislation would ensure that workers are not denied their day in court simply because they did not discover discrimination quickly enough. Democrats framed the measure as part of a broader economic agenda aimed at women and working families, arguing that unequal pay reduces household income, retirement security and long-term economic opportunity.

“Equal pay for equal work is not just a women’s issue — it is a family issue and an economic issue,” Pelosi and other supporters argued as the bill moved through Congress. They said the Supreme Court’s ruling had placed an unrealistic burden on employees by requiring them to challenge discriminatory pay decisions before they could reasonably know discrimination had occurred.

Republican critics and business groups warned that the bill could expose employers to lawsuits over decisions made many years earlier, making claims harder to defend as records disappear and witnesses leave. Supporters countered that the legislation does not guarantee victory for employees; it simply restores their ability to bring claims when discriminatory pay continues to affect their wages.

Ledbetter herself became a prominent advocate during the 2008 presidential campaign, appearing at the **Democratic National Convention** to tell her story and argue for changing the law. In one of the convention’s most memorable lines on the issue, she said: **“This fight became bigger than Lilly Ledbetter. Today, it’s about my daughter. It’s about my granddaughter. It’s about women and men across this country who deserve equal pay for equal work.”**

Her remarks helped turn the case into a national political symbol. Democrats cited her experience as evidence that legal protections had been weakened and needed to be restored. Then-Sen. Barack Obama supported the bill during the campaign, while Democrats used the issue to draw a contrast with Republicans on workplace rights and gender equality.

The measure’s passage marked a significant early test of the new Congress and the incoming Obama administration’s priorities. For civil rights advocates, labor unions and women’s organizations, the bill represented not only a reversal of the Supreme Court’s Ledbetter decision but also a reaffirmation of the principle that wage discrimination can persist — and compound — with every paycheck.

For Ledbetter, who never recovered the back pay the jury awarded because of the Supreme Court ruling, the legislation bearing her name was about ensuring that other workers would not face the same barrier.

The act’s core message, supporters said, is straightforward: when discrimination shows up in a paycheck, the law should recognize that harm — even if the first unfair decision was made years before.
